item.title: 2002: Scioscia, La Russa Named Managers of the Year
item.description: It was a busy manager awards day. First Mike Scioscia who led the Anaheim Angels to a 24-game turnaround from a 74-88 record in 2001 to a World Championship was named American League Manager of the Year, then Tony La Russa who led the Cardinals to 96 wins and overcoming with the deaths of Jack Buck and Darryl Kile to win the National League Central was named National League Manager of the Year. Photo: Googie man on en.wikipedia (CC BY-SA 3.0).

item.title: 2025: Paredes Elects Free Agency Following Season
item.description: Paredes elected free agency following the season on November 6, 2025. Photo: Sewageboy (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 2022: Blake Promoted to Pitching Coach for 2023 Season
item.description: On November 6, 2022, Blake was promoted to pitching coach for the 2023 season. Photo: Johnmaxmena2 (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 2020: Tigers Name Nieves Assistant Pitching Coach for 2021 Season
item.description: On November 6, 2020, the Detroit Tigers named Nieves as the team's assistant pitching coach for the 2021 season. Photo: Keith Allison (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2014: Dodgers Hire Farhan Zaidi as General Manager, Josh Byrnes as SVP
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers announce the hires of General Manager Farhan Zaidi and Senior Vice President/Baseball Operations Josh Byrnes. Zaidi joined the Oakland Athletics as a baseball operations analyst (2005) before holding the title of director of baseball operations (2009–13) with added duties of assistant general manager (2014).

item.title: 2013: Tigers Hire Clark as Third-Base Coach and Outfield Instructor
item.description: On November 6, 2013, the Tigers announced the hiring of Clark as third-base coach and outfield instructor. Photo: Keith Allison (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2013: Ace Parker, 101, Former Athletics Shortstop and NFL Star
item.description: Ace Parker, 101, shortstop who played 94 games for the 1937–1938 Philadelphia Athletics; at his death, the second oldest surviving Major League player; star football player for Duke University and three NFL teams, and member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 2011: Orioles Hire Dan Duquette, 53, as General Manager on Three-Year Deal
item.description: The Baltimore Orioles sign Dan Duquette to a three-year deal to become the general manager. Duquette, 53, was out of baseball since being dismissed by the Boston Red Sox in 2002. Photo: Keith Allison from Hanover, MD, USA (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2010: Ryan Signs Minor League Deal With Mets, Invited to Spring Training
item.description: On November 6, 2010 Ryan signed a minor league deal with the New York Mets with an invitation to Major League spring training. Photo: Skatefan on en.wikipedia (Public domain).

item.title: 2008: Hiroshima City Gives Mazda Naming Rights to Stadium
item.description: On November 6, 2008, Hiroshima City gave Mazda Motor Corporation naming rights to the stadium. Photo: HKT3012 (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 2001: Owners Vote 28-2 to Contract Twins and Expos
item.description: Major League Baseball owners vote 28–2 to contract two teams for the following season, with the Minnesota Twins and Montreal Expos—the teams expected to be eliminated—casting the dissenting votes. Photo: Bobak Ha'Eri (CC BY 3.0).

item.title: 2000: Sasaki, 32, Becomes Second-Oldest Rookie of the Year
item.description: Kazuhiro Sasaki of the Seattle Mariners, at the age of 32, becomes the second oldest major league player to be named rookie of the year. Only Sam Jethroe of the Boston Braves was older, Jethroe was 33 when he won the award in 1950.

item.title: 1997: Brewers Switch to National League Central Division
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers switch leagues, joining the National League Central Division, after the Kansas City Royals reject the invitation. With the 1998 addition of the Arizona Diamondbacks (NL) and Tampa Bay Devil Rays (AL), the move will maintain an even number of teams in each league.

item.title: 1990: Justice Named National League Rookie of the Year
item.description: Atlanta Braves outfielder David Justice was named National League Rookie of the Year.

item.title: 1989: Braves Sign Catcher Greg Olson, 29, as Free Agent
item.description: The Atlanta Braves sign catcher Greg Olson, granted free agency from the Minnesota Twins on October 15. Olson, 29, has played eight seasons in the minor leagues, with the exception of three games and five innings caught for the 1989 Twins. He'll become the 1990 Braves' most-used receiver, and be selected to the NL All-Star team. Photo: CandL and Colorcraft (Public domain).

item.title: 1987: Reds Trade Power and Stillwell to Royals for Jackson
item.description: The Cincinnati Reds trade pitcher Ted Power and shortstop Kurt Stillwell to the Kansas City Royals in exchange for pitcher Danny Jackson and infielder Ángel Salazar. The move allows the Reds to make Barry Larkin their new starting shortstop. Photo: Wknight94 (CC BY-SA 3.0).

item.title: 1980: Gorman Resigns as Mariners GM to Join Mets
item.description: Lou Gorman, the Seattle Mariners' most senior baseball executive from the expansion team's founding days in 1976, resigns as general manager to become vice president, baseball operations with the New York Mets. Working under Mets' GM and chief operating officer Frank Cashen, he'll play a key role in acquiring and developing talent for the club's mid-to-late 1980s National League powerhouse.

item.title: 1978: Yankees Unconditionally Release Andy Messersmith
item.description: Pitcher Andy Messersmith, the co-plaintiff with Dave McNally in the 1975 arbitration case that led to the Seitz decision and free agency, is unconditionally released by the New York Yankees. He will return to the Los Angeles Dodgers, the team he took to arbitration in the Seitz case, as a free agent in February 1979 and finish his career there.

item.title: 1976: Red Sox Sign Bill Campbell, 27, in First Free-Agent Move
item.description: The Boston Red Sox make the first move in the maiden free-agent market, signing former Minnesota Twins closer Bill Campbell to a four-year, $1 million contract. Campbell, 27, led the American League in games pitched (78), games finished (68) and winning percentage (.773), posting a 17–5 won–lost record and a 3.01 earned run average in 167<small>1/3</small> innings pitched.

item.title: 1974: Mike Marshall Wins Cy Young, First Relief Pitcher to Do So
item.description: Mike Marshall of the Los Angeles Dodgers wins the National League Cy Young Award—the first relief pitcher to do so. Marshall has just shattered his own MLB record for games pitched in a season, with 106. He went 15–12 (2.66) and led NL hurlers in games finished (83, a new MLB record) and saves (21).

item.title: 1968: Earl Gurley, Negro Leagues Outfielder and Pitcher, Dies
item.description: Earl Gurley, outfielder, first baseman and southpaw pitcher for seven clubs in the Negro leagues, chiefly the Memphis Red Sox, between 1922 and 1932.

item.title: 1948: Tigers Fire Steve O'Neill, Replace Him With Red Rolfe
item.description: The Detroit Tigers fire manager Steve O'Neill, at the helm since 1943, and replace him with former New York Yankees stalwart Red Rolfe, who had been Detroit's farm system director. O'Neill's 1945 Tigers won a pennant and World Series; Rolfe has five Fall Classic rings (1936–1939, 1941) from a decade spent with the Yankees as their four-time All-Star third baseman.

item.title: 1940: Greenberg Wins Second AL MVP With 16 First-Place Votes
item.description: The BBWAA elects Hank Greenberg of the pennant-winning Detroit Tigers the American League's Most Valuable Player for the second time in his career. With 16 of 24 first-place votes and 292 points, he outdistances Bob Feller (222 points with six first-place votes) of the league-runnerup Cleveland Indians. Greenberg led the AL in home runs (41) and runs batted in (150) this past season. Photo: Frank Lyerla (Public domain).

item.title: 1931: Jack Chesbro, 57, Hall of Fame Pitcher
item.description: Jack Chesbro, 57, Hall of Fame pitcher; a five-time 20-games winner in 12 seasons who led both leagues in wins and winning percentage, topped the National League in shutouts twice, guided the Pittsburgh Pirates to their first pennant in 1901 and the World Series in 1902, and holds modern records with 41 wins and 48 complete games while pitching for the 1904 New York Highlanders of the American League, though he is… Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1922: Morgan Bulkeley, 84, First National League President
item.description: Morgan G. Bulkeley, 84, executive who served as the National League's first president in 1876, also as president of Hartford club; later a governor of Connecticut and U.S. Senator. Photo: Osborn, Norris Galpin, b. 1858, ed (Public domain).

item.title: 1877: Lowell Ladies' Men Beat Boston 9-4, Win Inter-League Playoff
item.description: The Lowell Ladies' Men, pennant winners of the New England Association, defeat NL champion Boston, 9–4, to win the 1877 Inter-League playoff between the champions of the 2 leagues, 3 games to 1. Newspapers around the country did not use the term "World Series" yet, instead referring to the series sometimes as the "United States' Series" or the "Inter-League Exhibitions".

item.title: 1873: Philadelphia and Athletic Clubs Play Benefit Game With 10 Men
item.description: A crosstown benefit game is played between the Philadelphia and Athletic Clubs under a proposed rule of 10 men on the field and 10 innings for a game. The extra player is placed on the infield as a right shortstop and with most observers feeling the extra player unnecessary, the rule is never implemented. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).
